John Adams Confusion. Multiple historical figures named John or Adams from the early American era are frequently conflated. John Adams was the second United States president and Founding Father. His son John Quincy Adams was the sixth president. And Samuel Adams was a different Founding Father and organizer of the Boston Tea Party. These three figures are distinct and played different roles, yet their similar names and overlapping historical period cause confusion.

John Adams lived from 1735 to 1826. He was a diplomat, lawyer, and the second United States president from 1797 to 1801. He was a signer of the Declaration of Independence and a negotiator of the Treaty of Paris ending the Revolutionary War. Samuel Adams lived from 1722 to 1803 and was John Adams's cousin. He was a key organizer of anti-British resistance including the Boston Tea Party in 1773. He was a statesman but never served as president.

John Quincy Adams lived from 1767 to 1830 and was the son of John Adams. He served as the sixth United States president from 1825 to 1829. After his presidency, he served in the House of Representatives and was an abolitionist. The confusion intensifies because both John Adams and John Quincy Adams were presidents, making chronological and electoral distinctions easy to muddle.

Samuel Adams and John Adams were contemporaries and worked together during the Revolution, but Samuel Adams held fewer federal offices. He was a state politician in Massachusetts. John Quincy Adams outlived his father John Adams by three years. Both died in 1826, the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration of Independence—a notable coincidence that historically intertwines their legacies.
